lines.text: # Telegram delivery for `notifications` — closing the acceptance criterion
## Scope of this proposal
This is a proposal only. Nothing here has been run against a real Telegram
chat, nothing here writes to the ledger, `research/`, `gates/`, or
`pravrudhi_kernel/`, and no value in this proposal should be read as a
result. Where a script needs a stand-in credential or chat id it uses the
literal string `PLACEHOLDER`, never a number or token shape that could be
mistaken for a real one.
The task handed to this proposal names `research/telegram-bot-setup.md` as
the handoff doc with the exact code gap and diff. That path is
`.gitignore`d (`gates/`, `research/`, `.pravrudhi/` are all listed under
"local-only development and research documents" in `.gitignore`), so it
does not exist in this worktree — a fresh git worktree only contains
tracked files. This proposal could not read it and does not fabricate its
contents. Everything below is instead grounded in the three tracked source
files the operator's own gap description names directly:
`src/pravrudhi/application/notifications.py`, `messaging.py`, and
`reach.py`.
## What the tracked code actually shows today
Reading those three files in this worktree (commit `f60dd03`) shows the
delivery path already wired the way the acceptance criterion describes:
- `notifications.emit()` calls `_reach(root, note, engine_root)` after the
entry is written.
- `_reach()` imports `pravrudhi.application.messaging.resolve_telegram`,
calls it with `engine_root`, and — when it resolves — unpacks
`token, chat_id = resolved` and passes both into
`reach.send(root, kind=..., title=..., detail=..., token=token,
chat_id=chat_id)`.
- `messaging.resolve_telegram()` reads a stored per-root token first (the
BYOK path — see below), and only falls back to the process environment
(`TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN` / `TELEGRAM_CHAT_ID`, the systemd
`EnvironmentFile` path) when the caller names its own root as
`engine_root`. That is exactly the "operator-only environment
credential" boundary the operator's handoff describes.
So the specific line the operator's handoff calls out as missing —
`_reach()` never passing `token`/`chat_id` to `reach.send()` — is not
missing in this worktree's tracked source. Either the fix already landed
on this branch by the time this worktree was created, or the handoff
doc describes a different checkout. This proposal does not resolve that
discrepancy; it flags it so whoever has access to
`research/telegram-bot-setup.md` can diff its proposed patch against the
current `notifications.py`/`messaging.py`/`reach.py` before applying
anything, rather than re-applying a change that is already present.
## Two things worth fixing regardless, found while reading this path
1. **Naming**: the acceptance criterion is phrased around
`notifications.record()`. The tracked public API is
`notifications.emit()` (see its `__all__`). There is no `record`
function in this module. Whoever closes the criterion should either
correct the criterion's wording to `emit()`, or confirm a `record`
alias is expected and add one — but that is a one-line decision, not
a design question.
2. **Kind filter silently drops most `emit()` calls**: `reach.send()`
only delivers when `kind` is in `reach.DEFAULT_SEND_KINDS`, which is
exactly `{"promotion_needed", "audit_severity_high",
"pool_depleted"}`. `notifications.emit()`'s own docstring lists
example kinds — `run_finished`, `job_accepted`, `job_rejected`,
`job_cancelled`, `beat_dispatched`, `workflow_completed`,
`criterion_met` — almost none of which are in that filtered set. A
caller who records one of those kinds gets a correct ledger entry but
no Telegram message, silently (by design — `_reach` swallows
everything past the filter, and `reach.send` returns a `SendResult`
rather than raising). This is not a bug in the wiring the criterion
asks about, but it means a demonstration that uses a docstring-example
kind will look like a wiring failure when it is actually the intended
filter. Any evidence-gathering run must use a kind in
`DEFAULT_SEND_KINDS` (e.g. `promotion_needed`) or the filter must be
widened/configured first.
## BYOK / admin-only / auto-update notes carried over from the operator's request
The operator's message also asks for three product-policy points to be
recorded alongside the wiring work; they don't change the code in the
three files above; they change how it's exposed and operated:
- **BYOK, opt-in per workspace**: `messaging.set_telegram()` /
`telegram_status()` already implement exactly this — a workspace
stores its own token+chat id (refused inside a git worktree, written
0600) and only the engine's own root may additionally fall back to the
operator's environment credential. So "users bring their own bot, admin
uses the environment one" is already the shape of `messaging.py`; the
remaining work is a settings-UI affordance to call `set_telegram()`
from a user-facing screen, which is outside the three files read here
and outside this proposal's scope.
- **Pravrudhi Studio is admin-only**, not for other users or public
release. This is an access-control/deployment statement, not something
the telegram wiring touches; it belongs in whatever gate or deployment
policy document governs Studio's release channel, not in
`notifications.py`/`messaging.py`/`reach.py`.
- **Auto-update for the admin's Pravrudhi (the end-use build, not
Studio)** without operator intervention is a separate feature
(build/deploy automation) unrelated to the files this proposal read.
Recording it here only so it isn't lost: it should be its own proposal
against whatever module owns update/deploy, not bundled into the
telegram-delivery criterion.
## What would count as evidence this criterion is met
Two independent pieces, because this sandbox has no network access and
cannot produce either of them itself:
1. **An offline, no-network test of the call chain.** Something that
calls `notifications.emit(root, kind="promotion_needed", title=...,
engine_root=root)` against a temporary root with a resolvable
credential (either `messaging.set_telegram(root, token=..., chat_id=...)`
or `TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN`/`TELEGRAM_CHAT_ID` in the environment with
`engine_root == root`), with `httpx.post` patched so no real request
leaves the machine, and asserts the patched call received the
resolved `chat_id` and a request whose URL embeds the resolved token.
A passing run of that test is evidence the wiring is intact; it is
not evidence of real delivery, because Telegram itself is mocked out.
`verify_wiring_offline.py` in this directory sketches that test as a
proposal — it is not wired into the real test suite and asserts
nothing about a live chat.
2. **One human-observed real delivery**, run outside this sandbox by
someone with the operator's actual `~/.config/pravrudhi/telegram.env`
and engine root: call `notifications.emit()` (or whatever the
criterion's entry point is renamed to) with a kind in
`DEFAULT_SEND_KINDS`, and confirm two things by direct observation —
a message with the expected title/detail text arrives in the paired
Telegram chat, and the same entry appears in that engine root's
`.pravrudhi/notifications.jsonl`. Only that observation, recorded by
whoever can see both the ledger and the Telegram chat, closes the
criterion — this proposal cannot state a chat id, a token, or a
delivery outcome on the operator's behalf, and does not attempt to.
"""Proposal sketch, not a test run as evidence.
This is not wired into the real test suite and this proposal does not run it against a live
Telegram chat: this sandbox has no network access, and nothing produced here may be presented as
a result (see README.md). It sketches the offline, no-network check described in README.md's
"What would count as evidence" section: that `notifications.emit()` resolves a credential and
passes `token`/`chat_id` through to `reach.send()` -> `Sink._send_attempt()`, with the actual
HTTP call replaced by a stand-in so no request leaves the machine.
Every credential-shaped value below is the literal string PLACEHOLDER, never a plausible-looking
token or chat id, per this proposal's constraint against stating any number or outcome the ledger
does not contain.
To turn this into a real test, an integrator would drop it under `tests/`, import the actual
`notifications`, `messaging`, and `reach` modules, and run it with pytest and `unittest.mock.patch`
on `httpx.post`.
from __future__ import annotations
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Any
class FakeHttpResponse:
"""Stand-in for an `httpx.Response`, so no real HTTP call is made."""
def __init__(self, status_code: int, payload: dict[str, Any]) -> None:
self.status_code = status_code
self._payload = payload
self.headers = {"content-type": "application/json"}
def json(self) -> dict[str, Any]:
return self._payload
def sketch_offline_wiring_check(root: Path) -> dict[str, Any]:
"""Describe, without executing, the offline check an integrator would wire up.
Returns a plan (a dict of steps), not a result: this function does not import the real
`pravrudhi` package, does not patch `httpx.post`, and does not call `notifications.emit()`.
Doing any of that here would produce a number or an outcome this proposal is not allowed to
state. The plan below is what a real pytest test, added under `tests/`, would need to do.
return {
"root": str(root),
"credential_setup": (
"call messaging.set_telegram(root, token='PLACEHOLDER', chat_id='PLACEHOLDER') "
"so resolve_telegram(root, engine_root=root) resolves without touching the "
"process environment"
"patch_target": "httpx.post, so Sink._send_attempt() never opens a real connection",
"call_under_test": (
"notifications.emit(root, kind='promotion_needed', title='PLACEHOLDER', "
"engine_root=root) -- 'promotion_needed' is required because it is one of the "
"few kinds in reach.DEFAULT_SEND_KINDS; any other kind is filtered before send"
"assertions": [
"the patched httpx.post was called exactly once",
"the request URL contains the PLACEHOLDER token, not a real one",
"the request JSON body's chat_id equals the PLACEHOLDER chat id from set_telegram",
"the request JSON body's text contains the PLACEHOLDER title, MarkdownV2-escaped",
"out_of_scope_for_this_proposal": (
"asserting anything about a real Telegram chat, since this sandbox has no network "
"access and no such assertion could be evidence of anything"
if __name__ == "__main__":
plan = sketch_offline_wiring_check(Path("PLACEHOLDER"))
for step, description in plan.items():
print(f"{step}: {description}")
# Proposal: proving `alibaba-plan` resolves its own key and endpoint
Status: **draft only**. Nothing in this directory has been run against a live
credential or a live endpoint from here. This sandbox has no network access and
may not write to `research/`, `gates/`, `pravrudhi_kernel/`, or the ledger, so
nothing below is offered as a result — it is a design for the test that would
produce one, plus a note on what "reaching the endpoint" should mean.
## What already exists in the code (read, not changed, by this proposal)
`src/pravrudhi/agents/alibaba_agent.py` already separates the two Alibaba
surfaces by `provider_id`, not by a flag:
- `CREDENTIAL_NAMES = {"alibaba": "dashscope.env", "alibaba-plan": "dashscope-plan.env"}`
- `credential_path(provider_id)` returns `~/.config/llm/<that file>`, resolved
at call time.
- `credential(provider_id)` opens exactly that file (`O_NOFOLLOW`, must be an
owner-owned 0600 regular file) and reads the single `DASHSCOPE_API_KEY=...`
line from it. Both files use the same variable name; only the file chosen by
`provider_id` tells the two keys apart.
- `src/pravrudhi/application/credentials.py` gives the two provider ids
different `base_url`s: `alibaba` is
`https://dashscope-intl.aliyuncs.com/compatible-mode/v1` (free tier),
`alibaba-plan` is `https://token-plan.ap-southeast-1.maas.aliyuncs.com/compatible-mode/v1`
(the Lite Plan's own endpoint — plan keys are documented as rejected by the
free-tier host and vice versa, which is exactly the "reads like a bad key"
failure mode the module's own comment warns about).
- `configuration(model, provider_id)` writes that provider's `base_url` into
the OpenCode child config as `options.baseURL`, and the child process
receives the key only via the `DASHSCOPE_API_KEY` environment variable, never
on the command line.
`tests/test_alibaba_loop.py` already exercises this machinery offline (fake
`_run` transport, no network) for the default `alibaba` provider id: model
selection, the free-tier `baseURL`, redaction, credential file-mode
enforcement, and token accounting. It does not yet contain a case that (a)
selects `provider_id="alibaba-plan"`, (b) gives it a *different* key from a
*second*, distinct credential file, and (c) asserts the free-tier key is never
the one that reaches the plan endpoint. That gap is the oldest unmet criterion
this proposal targets, per the operator's note that the Lite Plan key is real
and already configured and that the two tiers must not be conflated.
## Approach
Add a test (sketched in `draft_test_alibaba_plan.py` in this directory,
following the existing fixture style in `tests/test_alibaba_loop.py`) that:
1. Fakes `Path.home()` to a `tmp_path`, and writes **two** credential files
under `<home>/.config/llm/`:
- `dashscope.env` containing a free-tier placeholder key, mode `0600`.
- `dashscope-plan.env` containing a *different* plan placeholder key, mode
Both use synthetic, obviously-fake values (`PLACEHOLDER`-style), never a
real secret — this directory has no business holding one.
2. Asserts `alibaba.credential("alibaba-plan").reveal()` equals the plan
file's value and differs from the free-tier file's value, so the file
chosen by `provider_id` — not the shared variable name — is what
distinguishes the two keys.
3. Builds `AlibabaAgent(root, provider_id="alibaba-plan")` (or
`build_agent(root, "opencode:alibaba-plan", model)`, whichever the registry
exposes), runs it through the existing fake `_run` transport, and inspects
exactly what the adapter would have handed the OpenCode child process:
- the `baseURL` embedded in `OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT` equals
`PROVIDERS["alibaba-plan"].base_url` (the plan-exclusive host), not
`PROVIDERS["alibaba"].base_url`;
- `env["DASHSCOPE_API_KEY"]` equals the **plan** key;
- the **free-tier** key string is asserted absent from `cmd`, `env`, and the
serialized config — a negative assertion, so the test fails loudly if the
two credential files were ever conflated (e.g. if `credential_path` or
`CREDENTIAL_NAMES` regressed to a single shared file).
4. Repeats step 3 symmetrically for `provider_id="alibaba"`, asserting the
plan key is absent, so the proof is bidirectional rather than only
"plan key reaches plan endpoint."
## What "reaches the plan-exclusive endpoint" should mean as evidence
This sandbox has no network access, so no run made here can show a real HTTP
round trip to `token-plan.ap-southeast-1.maas.aliyuncs.com`. Two tiers of
evidence follow from that constraint, and only the first is achievable inside
a no-network sandbox:
- **Offline/structural evidence** (what `draft_test_alibaba_plan.py` sketches):
proves the adapter *would* send the plan key to the plan `base_url` and
never to the free-tier `base_url`, by asserting on the exact `cmd`/`env`
passed to the (faked) OpenCode transport. This is the same style of proof
the existing suite already uses for the free tier, and it is what a unit
test can honestly claim.
- **Live confirmation**: a run, outside this sandbox, with network access and
the real `~/.config/llm/dashscope-plan.env` present, that dispatches
`AlibabaAgent(root, provider_id="alibaba-plan")` for real and records the
actual OpenCode transcript (as `ALIBABA_LOOP.md` already does for the
free-tier attempt) showing a completed turn against the plan endpoint. That
run, its transcript, and its pass/fail belong in the ledger by whoever has
the permissions and network access to produce them — not fabricated here as
a number.
This criterion is met only once both a test like
`draft_test_alibaba_plan.py` exists in `tests/`, is executed by the project's
real test runner, and its outcome is recorded in the ledger — none of which
this proposal round is permitted to do.
## On the operator's broader note
The operator's note that "the desktop app will not have access to any
api/routing for any model provider — they have to bring theirs" describes a
separate boundary from this credential test: end-user desktop installs
authenticate their own provider keys, while `~/.config/llm/dashscope-plan.env`
is specifically the Lite Plan credential used by Pravrudhi's own core/admin
agents (this `alibaba_agent` module, invoked from `pravrudhi_kernel`) — not a
credential ever handed to a desktop end user. This proposal only touches the
latter (the core-agent test), and does not modify anything under
`pravrudhi_kernel/`, `research/`, `gates/`, or `.pravrudhi/`, per the sandbox
policy for this round.
## Files here
- `README.md` — this document.
- `draft_test_alibaba_plan.py` — a draft pytest module in the style of
`tests/test_alibaba_loop.py`, meant to be reviewed and, if accepted, moved
into `tests/` and run for real. It has not been run from here.
"""DRAFT, unexecuted from this proposal round.
This sketches the test that would satisfy the criterion: that the
`alibaba-plan` provider resolves its key from `~/.config/llm/dashscope-plan.env`
under `DASHSCOPE_API_KEY`, that the request it builds targets the Lite Plan's
own endpoint, and that a key taken from the free-tier `dashscope.env` is never
sent to it (and symmetrically, the plan key is never sent to the free-tier
endpoint).
It follows the fixture style already used in `tests/test_alibaba_loop.py`
(fake `Path.home`, fake `_run` transport, no network). It is not part of the
project's real test suite: it lives under `proposals/` and is not collected by
the project's pytest configuration. Nothing here has been run against a real
credential or a real endpoint. Both key values below are synthetic
placeholders, not secrets.
To become evidence, this module (or its logic) would need to be reviewed,
moved into `tests/`, executed by the project's real test runner, and have its
outcome recorded in the ledger -- none of which this proposal round is
permitted to do.
from __future__ import annotations
import json
from pathlib import Path
import pytest
from pravrudhi.agents import alibaba_agent as alibaba
from pravrudhi.agents.registry import build_agent
from pravrudhi.application.credentials import PROVIDERS
FREE_TIER_KEY = "PLACEHOLDER-free-tier-key-not-a-secret"
PLAN_KEY = "PLACEHOLDER-lite-plan-key-not-a-secret"
def _write_credential(directory: Path, filename: str, key: str) -> Path:
path = directory / filename
path.write_text(f"DASHSCOPE_API_KEY={key}\n")
path.chmod(0o600)
return path
@pytest.fixture
def two_credential_files(tmp_path, monkeypatch):
"""A fake HOME holding both the free-tier and Lite Plan credential files."""
home = tmp_path / "home"
config_dir = home / ".config" / "llm"
config_dir.mkdir(parents=True)
monkeypatch.setattr(alibaba.Path, "home", lambda: home)
_write_credential(config_dir, "dashscope.env", FREE_TIER_KEY)
_write_credential(config_dir, "dashscope-plan.env", PLAN_KEY)
return home
def test_alibaba_plan_reads_its_own_file_not_the_free_tier_file(two_credential_files):
plan_secret = alibaba.credential("alibaba-plan")
free_secret = alibaba.credential("alibaba")
assert plan_secret.reveal() == PLAN_KEY
assert free_secret.reveal() == FREE_TIER_KEY
assert plan_secret.reveal() != free_secret.reveal()
def test_alibaba_plan_targets_the_plan_exclusive_endpoint():
plan_url = PROVIDERS["alibaba-plan"].base_url
free_url = PROVIDERS["alibaba"].base_url
assert plan_url != free_url
assert "token-plan" in plan_url
def test_dispatch_sends_only_the_plan_key_to_the_plan_endpoint(tmp_path, monkeypatch, two_credential_files):
"""Offline/structural proxy for "reaches the plan-exclusive endpoint".
No network is available in this sandbox, so this cannot show a real HTTP
round trip. What it can honestly show is that the adapter *would* send
the plan key, and only the plan key, to the plan `baseURL` -- and never
the free-tier key, by asserting on the exact command and environment the
(faked) OpenCode transport receives.
seen: dict[str, object] = {}
def transport(cmd, cwd, timeout_s, env):
seen["cmd"] = cmd
seen["env"] = env
return 0, json.dumps({"type": "step_finish", "sessionID": "s-1",
"part": {"reason": "stop"}}), "", 0.5
monkeypatch.setattr(alibaba, "_run", transport)
agent = build_agent(tmp_path, "opencode:alibaba-plan", "qwen-test")
agent.run("do it", tmp_path, timeout_s=12)
env = seen["env"]
config = json.loads(env["OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT"])
provider_config = config["provider"][alibaba.PROVIDER]

# IDE surface: pick Claude Code / Codex / OpenRouter per task
Status: design note only. Nothing here is implemented, and nothing here is a
result — every route id, provider id and field name below names something
that already exists in the checked-in source, cited by path, not a measured
outcome.
## What already exists (read, not guessed)
- **`configs/routing.yaml`** is the routing table the operator's request
called "routes.yaml". Each entry is a *route*: an `agent` (`claude-code`,
`codex`, `hosted`, `loop`, `orca:local`, ...), a `model`, the `tiers` it is
eligible for, and a `relative_cost` used to break ties. This is the table a
per-task picker would ultimately be choosing *from* — it is the source of
truth for "which agents exist and what tiers they may run at," not
something a UI should duplicate.
- **`/api/providers`** (`src/pravrudhi/api/server.py`, the `providers_ep`
handler) is the bring-your-own-key registry: for the calling user's
project, it reports each provider (`openai`, `anthropic`, `google`,
`alibaba`, `alibaba-plan`, `openai-compatible`, defined in
`src/pravrudhi/application/credentials.py`) as configured or not, never the
key itself. `POST /api/providers/{id}/key` and `DELETE
/api/providers/{id}/key` are how a key is set or removed. There is no
`openrouter` entry yet, but `openai-compatible` already models "an
OpenAI-shaped API with a base URL and a bearer key," which is exactly what
OpenRouter is — adding an `openrouter` provider (or a preset base URL on
`openai-compatible`) is a registry entry, not a new mechanism.
- **The swarm page** (`app/frontend/src/app/swarm/page.tsx`) already renders
a Dispatch section (`app/frontend/src/components/swarm/DispatchPanel.tsx`)
that lets an operator hand the swarm an ad hoc brief: title, brief, allowed
paths, validate command, tier, sandbox policy, and — already present today
— a free-text **"Pin an agent (optional)"** field. That field's value flows
straight through `JobInput.agent` (`app/frontend/src/lib/swarm.ts`) to
`POST /api/jobs`. In other words: the per-task "which agent handles this"
control the operator is asking for already has a seam in the UI and the
API; it is currently an unvalidated free-text box instead of a picker
backed by what is actually usable.
- The same page's `LivePanel`/`FleetTable`/`RoutingTable` already fetch
`/api/swarm`, whose response (`SwarmSnapshot` in `app/frontend/src/lib/
swarm.ts`) includes a `roster` of `Seat` objects — each seat already
carries `agent`, `model`, `tiers`, and a `usable` flag. That is close to,
but not the same as, "is this seat available to *this signed-in user*,"
because usability today reflects the operator's own configured routes and
quotas, not a per-user BYOK key.
## The gap
Nothing today lets a user, from the interface, say "run *this* task with
Claude Code" vs "with Codex" vs "with an OpenRouter model I've supplied a key
for," where the choice is constrained to options that will actually work for
*them* (their own configured provider keys) rather than a free-text field
that can name a route id that does not exist or is not usable by that
caller.
## Proposed approach
Extend, in this order, rather than build a parallel surface:
1. **No new backend route for the first slice.** The swarm page already
fetches both `/api/swarm` (for `roster`) and could fetch `/api/providers`
in the same load. Replace the DispatchPanel's free-text "Pin an agent"
input with a `<select>` populated from `roster`, each option showing
`agent` / `model` / `tier` eligibility, and disabled when the route's
underlying provider (matched by the route's `agent` field, e.g.
`claude-code` → `anthropic`, `codex` → `openai`, a prospective
`openrouter` route → `openrouter`) is not `configured` per
`/api/providers`. This is a frontend-only change: no schema change, no new
endpoint, because both data sources already exist and are already
fetched on adjacent parts of the same page.
2. **Second slice — validate server-side.** Today `dispatchboard.py`
presumably accepts `agent` as an opaque optional string (the API layer
already treats it that way per `JobInput.agent: string | null`). Add
server-side validation in the job-creation handler that rejects an
`agent`/route id that is not both (a) present in `configs/routing.yaml`
and (b) backed by a configured provider key for the caller, with a 422
and a reason — the same shape `set_provider_key` already uses for
validation failures. This turns "silently falls back to the router's
choice" into "tells the user why their pin was refused."
3. **Third slice — a dedicated `GET /api/routes`.** Once the picker needs
more than the swarm snapshot already provides (e.g. per-route
descriptions, or routes that are configured but not currently in the
roster because they've never been dispatched), add a small read-only
endpoint that joins `configs/routing.yaml` against the caller's
`/api/providers` configured set, so the frontend stops having to
cross-reference two responses itself. This is additive and does not
require touching the first two slices.
4. **OpenRouter specifically** needs one registry entry (`openrouter` in
`PROVIDERS`, `src/pravrudhi/application/credentials.py`, following the
`openai-compatible` shape with OpenRouter's base URL and key prefix) plus
one or more routes in `configs/routing.yaml` naming it as the `agent`
(however that agent is invoked — that plumbing is outside this note).
Nothing about the picker UI changes to support it: it is just another row
once the registry and routing table know about it.
The point of ordering it this way is that slice 1 ships with zero backend
change and turns an already-broken affordance (free text that can name
nothing real) into a working one, and each later slice is additive rather
than a rewrite of the one before it.
## What would count as evidence this criterion is met
This criterion is about the design note existing and being accurate, not
about the feature shipping. Evidence would be:
- This README (or its successor) accurately naming the extension points —
`configs/routing.yaml`, `/api/providers`, the swarm page's DispatchPanel —
against whatever those files contain at review time, since they are
expected to keep moving.
- A reviewer being able to trace, from this note alone, exactly which
existing file each proposed slice touches and which fields it reads, with
no invented endpoint or field that is not either (a) cited above as
already existing or (b) explicitly marked as new in "Proposed approach."
- The smallest slice (item 1) being buildable without any change outside
`app/frontend/src/components/swarm/DispatchPanel.tsx` and, if the fetch is
added there, `app/frontend/src/lib/swarm.ts` — i.e. that the claim "no
backend change needed for the first slice" holds up when someone tries it.
- This directory containing no implementation of the picker itself — only
the sketch in `sketch_routes_view.py`, which documents shapes and is not
wired into the running application.
## Files here
- `README.md` — this note.
- `sketch_routes_view.py` — a non-executable sketch (dataclasses only, no
logic, no network, no imports from `pravrudhi_kernel`/`src`) of the shapes
a future `GET /api/routes` response and the picker's option list might
take, to make slice 3 concrete without writing the endpoint.

# Proposal: agent-orchestration framework comparison for Pravrudhi
Request `r-4b5cdaf1`. Operator's words (part 1 of a four-part ask): "research and setup
multiple agent orchestration systems (langgraph, openai/claude/google agent sdk etc)..
there are a lot on the market. this is what will make pravrudhi an ade too behind the
rsi.....implement the best-leverage open source implementations...stake this as another
objective for pravrudhi."
This document is a proposal only. Nothing here writes to the ledger, `research/`,
`gates/`, or `pravrudhi_kernel/`, no package was installed, and no code from any of the
six frameworks was written or run. No number in this document is a claimed result — where
the underlying criterion asks for "integration cost in files touched," this proposal
answers with named modules/entrypoints, not a file count, because a count would read as a
measured outcome this sandbox is not allowed to state.
This folder previously held a proposal for a different part of the same operator ask (the
builder/product naming-demarcation criterion). That content has been superseded here
because the oldest unmet criterion for this request is now this one — the framework
comparison — not naming. It is not lost: it was tracked on this branch's history before
being replaced, so a reviewer who needs it can recover it from that history; this sandbox
may only hold one active deliverable at this path at a time.
## What this sandbox could and couldn't do
This sandbox has no network access, so nothing below was fetched live. Every URL cited is
a canonical, stable documentation or repository-license location for the named framework,
cited from general knowledge of how each project publishes its docs and license, exactly
as the criterion asks: "every claim cites the framework's own docs by URL." A reviewer
with network access should confirm each URL still resolves to the claim attributed to it
before treating this comparison as settled.
This sandbox also does not read `pravrudhi_kernel/` (out of scope for a proposal, and not
named by this task). So "Pravrudhi's own swarm/delegate/heartbeat" is treated here at the
level the operator's own vocabulary already describes it — swarm as the fan-out primitive
that runs many agents over one task, delegate as the handoff primitive that transfers a
task from one agent to another, heartbeat as the liveness/resumption primitive that keeps
a long-running objective moving — not as an audited reading of the kernel source. Every
"what it would replace or wrap here" and "integration cost in files touched" line below is
a proposed mapping onto that vocabulary, flagged for confirmation by whoever has
`pravrudhi_kernel/` read access, not an audited fact.
## Approach
1. **Structured data first, prose second.** `frameworks.yaml` holds one entry per
framework named in the criterion (LangGraph, OpenAI Agents SDK, Claude Agent SDK,
Google ADK, CrewAI, AutoGen), each with: `license` + `license_url`, `docs_url` (plus
more specific `*_docs_url` fields for individual claims), `core_model` (what the
framework actually is, one paragraph), `replace_or_wrap` (a single verdict:
Pravrudhi would replace its own primitive with this framework's equivalent, or wrap
the framework's primitive around Pravrudhi's own), `pravrudhi_touchpoints` (which of
swarm/delegate/heartbeat it would touch), `integration_notes`, and
`files_touched_categories` (named modules/entrypoints, never a count). The file also
carries a single `recommendation` block naming one pick and the reasons for it.
2. **A schema/citation checker, not a scorer.** `scripts/validate_comparison.py` loads
`frameworks.yaml` and checks that every entry has the fields above populated, that
every URL is `https://`, that `replace_or_wrap` is one of the two allowed verdicts,
that `pravrudhi_touchpoints` only names swarm/delegate/heartbeat, and — specifically
to keep the "no number presented as a result" rule structural rather than just
promised in prose — that no `files_touched_categories` entry contains a digit. It
prints a PASS/FAIL line per framework and returns a process exit code; it does not
print or compute any score.
3. **One recommendation, with reasons, not a ranked list.** The criterion asks for "one
recommendation with reasons," so `frameworks.yaml`'s `recommendation` block names
exactly one framework and gives the reasons, rather than scoring all six against each
other numerically.
## The comparison
| Framework | Licence | Would replace or wrap | Pravrudhi touchpoint(s) |
| [LangGraph](https://langchain-ai.github.io/langgraph/) | [MIT](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph/blob/main/LICENSE) | wrap | swarm |
| [OpenAI Agents SDK](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/) | [MIT](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/main/LICENSE) | wrap | delegate |
| [Claude Agent SDK](https://docs.claude.com/en/api/agent-sdk/overview) | [MIT](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-agent-sdk-python/blob/main/LICENSE) | wrap | delegate, heartbeat |
| [Google ADK](https://google.github.io/adk-docs/) | [Apache-2.0](https://github.com/google/adk-python/blob/main/LICENSE) | wrap | swarm, heartbeat |
| [CrewAI](https://docs.crewai.com/) | [MIT](https://github.com/crewAIInc/crewAI/blob/main/LICENSE) | replace (for the parts touched) | heartbeat |
| [AutoGen](https://microsoft.github.io/autogen/) | [MIT](https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/blob/main/LICENSE) | wrap | swarm |
Full reasoning, the specific docs URL backing each claim, and the named
files-touched-categories per framework are in `frameworks.yaml` — this table is a summary
view of that file, not a second source of truth.
### Recommendation
**Claude Agent SDK.** Reasons (full text in `frameworks.yaml`'s `recommendation` block):
- This session's own tool surface — an Agent tool for spawning subagents, a
hooks-driven session lifecycle, a self-paced resumption primitive — is already an
instance of this SDK's own documented subagent/hook model
(https://docs.claude.com/en/api/agent-sdk/subagents). Adopting it narrows existing
custom glue down to the SDK's own primitives instead of introducing a second
orchestration model that would need to be reconciled with the kernel's ledger.
- It is the only one of the six proposed here to touch both delegate and heartbeat at
once, without asking Pravrudhi to hand ownership of the swarm dispatcher or the ledger
to an external framework's persistence/process model, the way LangGraph's checkpointer,
Google ADK's `sub_agents` tree, or CrewAI's Process would.
- Licence (MIT) is not the differentiator: four of the six candidates share it. The
integration-cost and touchpoint arguments above are what carry the recommendation.
This recommendation, like every touchpoint mapping above, is a proposal for a reviewer
with `pravrudhi_kernel/` read access to confirm — see "What this sandbox could and
couldn't do."
## What would count as evidence this criterion is met
None of the following can be produced from inside this sandbox:
1. **The comparison is reviewed and each cited URL confirmed to say what this document
claims it says**, by someone with network access, against the live framework docs
rather than this proposal's recollection of them.
2. **Each `pravrudhi_touchpoints` and `files_touched_categories` mapping is checked
against the real `pravrudhi_kernel/` source** by someone with read access to it, and
corrected where this proposal's outside-in reading of swarm/delegate/heartbeat
diverges from how the kernel actually implements them.
3. **The recommended framework is staked as an objective**, per the operator's
instruction ("stake this as another objective for pravrudhi") — i.e., a new objective
file exists (outside this sandbox, likely alongside `prabhasa-nyaya.yaml` and
`sanghatana-yoga`-style objectives) that names the Claude Agent SDK wrap as work to be
done, with acceptance criteria a future gate can check against the ledger.
4. **`uv run python -m compileall -q .` and the existing gate suite continue to pass**
after any of the above lands — this proposal does not ask anyone to break existing
behavior to adopt a framework.

# primitives by the operator's own vocabulary for them; this sandbox does not
# read pravrudhi_kernel/, so treat each touchpoint as a proposed mapping for a
# reviewer with kernel read access to confirm, not an audited fact.
frameworks:
- name: LangGraph
license: MIT
license_url: https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph/blob/main/LICENSE
docs_url: https://langchain-ai.github.io/langgraph/
primitive_docs_url: https://langchain-ai.github.io/langgraph/concepts/low_level/
persistence_docs_url: https://langchain-ai.github.io/langgraph/concepts/persistence/
core_model: >
A graph of nodes and edges with built-in state persistence and
checkpointing, meant for stateful, cyclic, multi-step agent workflows.
replace_or_wrap: wrap
pravrudhi_touchpoints: [swarm]
integration_notes: >
Its `Send` API (see primitive_docs_url) is a natural wrap for
Pravrudhi's swarm fan-out step: model one swarm dispatch as one
LangGraph superstep. Adopting more than that means reconciling
LangGraph's own checkpointer (persistence_docs_url) with Pravrudhi's
ledger, which is a competing source of truth, not a wrap.
files_touched_categories:
- the swarm dispatch entrypoint
- an adapter boundary between LangGraph's checkpointer and the ledger
(only if persistence is not disabled)
- name: OpenAI Agents SDK
license: MIT
license_url: https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/main/LICENSE
docs_url: https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/
primitive_docs_url: https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/handoffs/
models_docs_url: https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/models/
core_model: >
Agents, Handoffs, Guardrails and Sessions, run through the SDK's own
Runner loop, with pluggable model providers (models_docs_url).
replace_or_wrap: wrap
pravrudhi_touchpoints: [delegate]
integration_notes: >
Handoffs (primitive_docs_url) are conceptually the closest analogue to
Pravrudhi's delegate primitive: one agent transferring a task and
control to another. The cost is that the SDK expects to own the
model-call loop itself, so wrapping delegate means routing whichever
model calls go through delegate via the SDK's Runner instead of
Pravrudhi's own call path.
files_touched_categories:
- the delegate handoff interface
- wherever Pravrudhi currently issues the model call that delegate
hands off to
- name: Claude Agent SDK
license: MIT
license_url: https://github.com/anthropics/claude-agent-sdk-python/blob/main/LICENSE
docs_url: https://docs.claude.com/en/api/agent-sdk/overview
subagents_docs_url: https://docs.claude.com/en/api/agent-sdk/subagents
core_model: >
The same harness this proposal is itself being written under: agents,
subagents, tools, hooks and permission modes (docs_url,
subagents_docs_url).
replace_or_wrap: wrap
pravrudhi_touchpoints: [delegate, heartbeat]
integration_notes: >
This session's own tool surface (an Agent tool for spawning subagents,
a hooks-driven SessionStart/Stop lifecycle, a ScheduleWakeup primitive
for self-paced resumption) is already an instance of this SDK's
documented subagent and hook model (subagents_docs_url). Subagents map
directly onto delegate; hooks map directly onto heartbeat (liveness /
resumption signalling). Because Pravrudhi already runs on this harness,
adoption here is narrowing custom glue code down to the SDK's own
primitives, not introducing a second orchestration model to reconcile
with the kernel's ledger.
files_touched_categories:
- the delegate handoff interface, where it currently reimplements
subagent dispatch by hand
- the heartbeat scheduler, where it currently reimplements
hook-driven resumption by hand
- name: Google ADK
license: Apache-2.0
license_url: https://github.com/google/adk-python/blob/main/LICENSE
docs_url: https://google.github.io/adk-docs/
workflow_agents_docs_url: https://google.github.io/adk-docs/agents/workflow-agents/
multi_agent_docs_url: https://google.github.io/adk-docs/agents/multi-agents/
core_model: >
Agents plus workflow agents (SequentialAgent, ParallelAgent,

replace_or_wrap: wrap
pravrudhi_touchpoints: [swarm, heartbeat]
integration_notes: >
ParallelAgent maps onto swarm's fan-out and LoopAgent maps onto
heartbeat's poll-until-condition shape (workflow_agents_docs_url).

agent tree via sub_agents, so folding delegate in as well means
migrating Pravrudhi's agent registry into that tree rather than
wrapping it.

- the swarm dispatch entrypoint
- the heartbeat scheduler
- the agent registry (only if delegate is folded in too)
- name: CrewAI

docs_url: https://docs.crewai.com/
flows_docs_url: https://docs.crewai.com/concepts/flows

core_model: >
Crews (role-based agent teams with a Process: sequential or

pravrudhi_touchpoints: [heartbeat]
integration_notes: >
Flows' event/state-driven progression is the only piece that sits near

core_model: >
Conversable agents composed into a GroupChat (groupchat_docs_url),

replace_or_wrap: wrap
pravrudhi_touchpoints: [swarm]
integration_notes: >
GroupChat's many-agents-in-one-exchange model is a plausible narrow

termination conditions (termination_docs_url) are only a loose fit for
heartbeat — adopting AutoGen for either would need custom glue code,
not just a wrap.

recommendation:
pick: Claude Agent SDK
reasons:
Lowest integration cost of the group: this session's own tool surface
(Agent tool, hooks, ScheduleWakeup) is already an instance of this
SDK's documented subagent/hook model (see
frameworks[name=Claude Agent SDK].subagents_docs_url), so adoption
narrows existing custom glue down to the SDK's own primitives instead
of introducing a second orchestration model.
It is the only one of the six with a proposed touchpoint on both
delegate and heartbeat at once, without requiring Pravrudhi to give up
ownership of the swarm dispatcher or the ledger the way LangGraph's
checkpointer, ADK's sub_agents tree, or CrewAI's Process would.
Permissive MIT license (frameworks[name=Claude Agent SDK].license_url),
same as four of the other five candidates, so license is not a
differentiator here — the integration-cost and touchpoint arguments
are what carry the recommendation.

This recommendation is a proposal for a reviewer with pravrudhi_kernel/
read access to check, not a verified audit: this sandbox does not read
pravrudhi_kernel/, so every pravrudhi_touchpoints mapping above is
inferred from the operator's own swarm/delegate/heartbeat vocabulary and
from this session's own observable tool surface, not from the kernel
source.
"""Schema/citation completeness check for frameworks.yaml.
This does not evaluate whether the comparison is *correct* — that is a
judgment call for a human reviewer. It only checks the structural promise
this proposal makes: that every framework entry names a licence with a
source URL, docs with a source URL, a replace-or-wrap verdict, at least one
proposed Pravrudhi touchpoint, and a files_touched_categories list (never a
files_touched *count*, since a count would read as a measured result this
sandbox is not allowed to state).
Exit status is PLACEHOLDER-free: this script prints a per-framework
PASS/FAIL label and returns a process exit code, never a numeric score.
import sys
from pathlib import Path
import yaml
REQUIRED_FRAMEWORK_FIELDS = (
"name",
"license",
"license_url",
"docs_url",
"core_model",
"replace_or_wrap",
"pravrudhi_touchpoints",
"integration_notes",
"files_touched_categories",
VALID_TOUCHPOINTS = {"swarm", "delegate", "heartbeat"}
VALID_VERDICTS = {"replace", "wrap"}
def load(path: Path) -> dict:
with path.open("r", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
return yaml.safe_load(fh)
def check_framework(entry: dict) -> list[str]:
problems = []
for field in REQUIRED_FRAMEWORK_FIELDS:
value = entry.get(field)
if value in (None, "", []):
problems.append(f"missing or empty field: {field}")
for url_field in ("license_url", "docs_url"):
url = entry.get(url_field, "")
if url and not url.startswith("https://"):
problems.append(f"{url_field} is not an https URL: {url!r}")
verdict = entry.get("replace_or_wrap")
if verdict is not None and verdict not in VALID_VERDICTS:
problems.append(f"replace_or_wrap not one of {VALID_VERDICTS}: {verdict!r}")
touchpoints = entry.get("pravrudhi_touchpoints") or []
unknown = sorted(set(touchpoints) - VALID_TOUCHPOINTS)
if unknown:
problems.append(f"unknown pravrudhi_touchpoints: {unknown}")
for item in entry.get("files_touched_categories") or []:
if any(ch.isdigit() for ch in item):
problems.append(
f"files_touched_categories entry contains a digit "
f"(should name a module, not a count): {item!r}"
return problems
def check_recommendation(data: dict) -> list[str]:
rec = data.get("recommendation")
if not rec:
return ["missing top-level 'recommendation'"]
problems = []
if not rec.get("pick"):
problems.append("recommendation.pick is empty")
if not rec.get("reasons"):
problems.append("recommendation.reasons is empty")
names = {f["name"] for f in data.get("frameworks", [])}
if rec.get("pick") not in names:
problems.append(
f"recommendation.pick {rec.get('pick')!r} is not one of the "
f"compared frameworks {sorted(names)}"
return problems
def main() -> int:
here = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
data = load(here / "frameworks.yaml")
frameworks = data.get("frameworks", [])
all_ok = True
for entry in frameworks:
name = entry.get("name", "<unnamed>")
problems = check_framework(entry)
if problems:
all_ok = False
print(f"FAIL {name}")
for p in problems:
print(f"  - {p}")
else:
print(f"PASS {name}")
rec_problems = check_recommendation(data)
if rec_problems:
all_ok = False
print("FAIL recommendation")
for p in rec_problems:
print(f"  - {p}")
else:
print("PASS recommendation")
return 0 if all_ok else 1
if __name__ == "__main__":
sys.exit(main())

objectives.intent: A scaffolding harness that makes a fixed model write correct Python more often, changed only in how the model is prompted and how its output is checked, never in the model's weights.
objectives.notes: The internal pool selected a harness change that the external scorer then contradicted. That contradiction is in the ledger and this objective renders it rather than hiding it; a promotion the external tier refuses is the most useful row the loop has produced.

objectives.intent: A small model that solves grade-school arithmetic word problems more reliably than the checkpoint it started from, without losing what it already knew.
objectives.notes: Scored by lm-evaluation-harness outside the kernel, on the held-out test split, and admitted to the ledger by file hash. The internal sealed pool is the loop's selection instrument and is not this objective's evidence.

objectives.intent: An orchestration strategy that makes a fixed model solve more programming problems correctly, changed only in how work is decomposed, dispatched, checked and retried across one or more agents, never in the model's weights. The engine's own single-agent harness is the incumbent every candidate is paired against, so a strategy that adds coordination without adding correctness is visible as such rather than assumed better.
objectives.notes:
What a candidate is: a named strategy expressed in the harness grammar. A single agent with retries is the incumbent. A planner that decomposes then executes, a proposer-and-critic pair, a fan-out that solves the same problem several ways and selects, and a graph with explicit state between steps are all candidates, and each is what the frameworks on the market actually implement underneath their APIs.
Adopting a framework is therefore the second question, not the first. If decomposition beats a single agent on these benchmarks, the framework that expresses decomposition well is worth its dependency; if it does not, no framework's ergonomics will help, and this engine will have learned that for the price of a few nights rather than a rewrite.
The likeliest outcome, stated in advance so its arrival is informative rather than disappointing: coordination costs tokens and adds failure modes, and on problems a single agent already solves it will lose. The interesting result would be a strategy that wins specifically on the problems the incumbent fails, which is a question about where the gains are rather than whether the mean moved.

objectives.intent: A legal-reasoning assistant for Indian jurisprudence that answers a question of law with the statute or precedent it relied on, and that says it does not know rather than inventing a citation. The reasoning is to run over a typed Nyaya meaning graph rather than over surface text, so that a wrong answer can be traced to the inference step that produced it.
objectives.notes: Cited-statute accuracy is the metric this objective actually wants and no public harness scores it. The two MMLU law subtasks are stand-ins that move for the right reasons; treat them as a proxy and say so, rather than reporting them as if they measured citation faithfulness.

rows.notes: GitHub is reached only to check for releases. There is no repository browsing, issue or pull request surface.
rows.why_it_matters: Review and land work without switching to a browser.

rows.notes: Five backends resolve on this machine, and one of them drives Orca itself. Routing picks between them from measured outcomes rather than a fixed preference.
rows.why_it_matters: Use the agent that suits the task rather than the one the app ships with.

rows.capability: Direct visual editing of an interface
rows.notes: Not built and not currently planned. Listed so the gap is visible rather than absent.
rows.why_it_matters: Change a layout by pointing at it instead of describing it.

rows.capability: Work on a remote machine over SSH
rows.notes: Hosts are surveyed for accelerator, memory and installed agents, so a task can be placed on a machine that can actually run it.
rows.why_it_matters: Use the machine that has the hardware.

rows.capability: Drag a file into the conversation
rows.notes:
A file dropped on the composer is read in the browser and its text folded into the message, since this engine has no upload route and none was added. The limits are therefore the whole of the protection and are stated as named constants with their reasons: 256 KB a file, 512 KB in total, four at once, text and source formats only. Every refusal carries its own sentence rather than failing silently.
The evidence names the page as well as the components, deliberately. They existed for a while mounted on nothing, exactly as the command palette once did, and this row stayed at none for as long as that was true.
rows.why_it_matters: Attach context without typing a path.

rows.notes: A note attaches to a file and line of a task's diff, several to a line, and the set for a task reads as a whole because the reason to write them is to hand them to someone. They live in the browser: an annotation is one reviewer's working note, the engine has no route to store one, and a blocked storage API degrades to notes that last the session rather than breaking the page.
rows.why_it_matters: Say what is wrong with a change at the line it is wrong on.

rows.capability: A command line for the whole product
rows.notes: Thirty-two commands, covering the whole loop rather than a chat wrapper.
rows.why_it_matters: Script the tool and use it over a plain SSH session.

rows.notes: Ctrl+K opens the palette over pages, actions and records; digits 1-9 reach the sidebar directly; "/" focuses the page's own input; "?" lists every shortcut; Escape closes the topmost layer only, which is the part with a test rather than a screenshot. A key pressed while typing is left to the field it was typed into.
rows.why_it_matters: Work without reaching for the pointer.

rows.notes: Keys can be supplied per provider and are stored outside the work tree at 0600. There is no notion of two accounts for one provider, and no switch in the interface.
rows.why_it_matters: Separate work from personal quota, and survive one account being rate limited.

rows.capability: Edit a document in the application
rows.notes: A note is written, corrected in place and deleted, with a Markdown source/preview editor over a renderer whose escaping and scheme allowlist are tested as attacks. The claim is the round trip rather than the widget - the editor existed for a while with its Save button wired to nothing, which is why the evidence is the API test and the page's handler rather than the component's presence.
rows.why_it_matters: Keep notes and plans where the work is.

rows.capability: Choose the agent and model from measured outcomes
rows.notes: A route is picked as the cheapest whose Wilson interval upper bound still reaches the best route's lower bound, so a cheap route is kept until the log can actually tell them apart. The claim is the rule and its recorded outcomes, not that the ranking is correct - on 2026-09-08 the Lite Plan seat stood at two successes in six trials, an interval of 0.10 to 0.70, which distinguishes it from nothing yet.
rows.why_it_matters: Spend on the expensive route only once the evidence distinguishes it from a cheaper one.

rows.capability: Every stated number traces to an append-only ledger row
rows.notes: The ledger is written once and verified as a chain, and replay folds it back into the state a night saw. The scope is the mechanism; it does not assert that every surface in the product reads from it.
rows.why_it_matters: A result that cannot be replayed from its own record is a claim, not a measurement.

rows.capability: Read back the parent structure of the search
rows.notes: The lineage field was written on every proposal from the start and read by nothing. Folded, the committed ledger gives 189 candidates, two distinct parents and a maximum depth of two - a two-node star, which is recorded here as the shape the search currently has rather than as an achievement.
rows.why_it_matters: Without ancestry an evolutionary arm has nothing to shrink toward and no novelty to reward.

rows.capability: Report whether the budget forced a choice at all
rows.notes: Per night, the live pool against what was run. On the committed ledger the budget bound on seven of sixteen nights, so on the other nine the controller ranked a set it was going to run in full. This row exists to keep that measurable; it is the least flattering number the engine reports about itself.
rows.why_it_matters: A selection rule earns nothing on a night when everything proposed could be afforded.

rows.capability: Run unattended within a declared appetite
rows.notes: A night proposes, measures and prunes without intervention, and the drives that choose what to do next are weighted by a checked-in appetite policy an operator can override per workspace. The claim is that it runs unattended and bounded, not that any given night improved anything.
rows.why_it_matters: Improvement that needs an operator present is not improvement the operator can leave running.

objectives.intent: A legal-reasoning assistant for Indian jurisprudence that answers a question of law with the statute or precedent it relied on, and that says it does not know rather than inventing a citation. Reasoning runs over a typed Nyaya meaning graph rather than surface text, so a wrong answer can be traced to the inference step that produced it.
objectives.notes: Proxies are labelled as proxies. Cited-statute accuracy is what this objective wants; the law benchmarks move for related reasons and must never be reported as measuring citation faithfulness. The reasoning-versus-recall gap (sr-question-only against professional-law) is the closest available proxy for the product's actual claim.

completion gate refused: ## Finding: criterion [0] fails — no agent actually persists on parity; the only autonomous loop explicitly excludes it

I read the cited evidence file (`completion.py`) and traced where "parity" actually lives in the codebase, since `completion.py` itself contains nothing about Orca, parity, or rivalry — it's a generic evidence-verification/adversarial-review gate applicable to any request.

The real parity machinery is `src/pravrudhi/application/parity.py` + `src/pravrudhi/assets/configs/parity.yaml`: a hand-edited YAML capability matrix with self-checking evidence (`grep`/test commands), exposed read-only through a CLI command (`pravrudhi parity`) and `/api/parity`. Nothing in that path is an agent that *persists* — it's a static table a human (or an ad hoc agent session) edits when prompted.

The one candidate for an actual persistent/autonomous agent is the heartbeat (`src/pravrudhi/application/heartbeat.py`, driven by `pravrudhi-heartbeat.timer`), which wakes on a schedule and dispatches work against the engine's six-then-seven "drives" in `kshudha.py`. Rivalry against named competitors is modeled there as `spardha_drive` (kshudha.py:394) — but it computes gaps only against *declared benchmark scores* (e.g. GSM8K), not UX/feature parity, and it is not wired into the heartbeat's dispatch table at all: `heartbeat.py`'s `_action_for` only handles `samarthya`, `seva`, `sthiti`, with `sadhana` falling back to a no-op desire log and `pramana_navyata`/`unnati_avakasha` explicitly producing "a bounded diagnostic, never a fabricated [action]." `spardha` doesn't appear in `_action_for` at all — grepping `heartbeat.py` for `spardha` returns nothing.

The codebase's own commentary in `parity.yaml` concedes this directly: it notes OpenClaw has "an autonomous loop that executes (autonomousLoop.js) where this engine's heartbeat only chooses" — i.e., the project's own record states that, unlike the rival being compared against, nothing here turns a parity gap into dispatched, executed work on its own. The OpenClaw row itself was filled in only after "the completion gate's adversarial reviewer correctly called out" that it had sat at `unknown` despite being named twice — meaning the parity table's accuracy depends on someone manually noticing the gap and then manually researching and hand-editing the YAML, not on a dedicated agent that persists on the work.

So criterion [0]'s evidence file does not establish what it claims. There is a parity *report* and a generic evidence-verification *gate*, but no agent — scheduled or otherwise — whose job is to keep working toward closing feature/UX gaps against Orca (or Claude Desktop, Codex, OpenClaw). This does not satisfy the operator's explicit ask to "dedicate an agent to persist on it."

## Secondary finding: criterion [3]'s "real clicks" demo is a static slideshow, not an interactive demonstration

`app/frontend/src/app/tour/page.tsx` renders a fixed sequence of 10 steps from one static JSON snapshot (`loadTour()`), advancing on a button or a 7-second autoplay timer — there is no simulated clicking, no live interaction, and no video. The desktop-specific step (`StepDesktop.tsx`) is a single static screenshot with a caption that explicitly says it was "caught mid-update-check before anyone clicked anything" — the opposite of showing "real clicks" and "how the desktop app updates." This is a scripted walkthrough of a recording, not a demo of the desktop app updating in real time as the operator asked for.

## Overall

Given the operator's explicit demand for a dedicated persisting parity agent and a demo with real interaction, criterion [0] does not hold, and criterion [3]'s evidence overstates what it shows. This does not satisfy what was asked.

completion gate refused: ## Finding: criterion [0]/[1] — "every operator ask" is not actually captured by Pravrudhi

The evidence for criterion [0] cites `src/pravrudhi/application/requests.py` as proof that "every operator ask is captured in a log inside Pravrudhi." Reading that module shows it is a well-built, passive data layer: a `Request`/`Criterion` dataclass model, a JSON store under `.pravrudhi/requests.json`, a state machine, and a `capture()` function — but `capture()` only runs when something calls it. The module itself has no listener on any input channel; it cannot capture anything on its own.

I traced what actually calls `capture()`/`requests-capture` in the shipped code:

- `src/pravrudhi/application/watchdog.py` and `src/pravrudhi/application/telegram_inbox.py` call it directly.
- `pravrudhi/cli/app.py` exposes it as `requests-capture`, a CLI command someone (or something) must invoke.
- Pravrudhi's own chat surface, `src/pravrudhi/application/chat.py` (the very file cited in criterion [5] as the engine's first-person voice), **never calls `capture` at all** — a `grep` for `capture` in that file returns nothing.

The actual mechanism that makes "every ask you type to me right now" land in the ledger is `.claude/hooks/capture-ask.py`, registered via `.claude/settings.json` as a `UserPromptSubmit` hook, which shells out to `pravrudhi requests-capture`. I confirmed with `git check-ignore -v` that **both `.claude/` (the hook and its registration) and `.pravrudhi/` (the ledger file itself) are gitignored** by this repository's own `.gitignore` (lines 14–15). None of this ships with Pravrudhi. A fresh clone, a different machine, a different agent in the swarm (Codex, Astra, the desktop app), or this same operator talking to Pravrudhi through any surface other than this specific Claude Code session on this specific machine, has no automatic capture at all.

Even where the hook is installed, it does not capture "every" ask by its own documented design (confirmed against the operator's own prior memory note on this exact mechanism): it skips prompts under 80 characters, skips prompts containing harness markers, skips near-duplicates, and **swallows every failure silently** — so if the hook script breaks, asks stop being recorded with no signal from inside Pravrudhi that anything was missed. The memory record documents this already happened once: five substantial asks went uncaptured in one afternoon.

So the acceptance criterion's evidence is real and the cited code is solid, but it demonstrates a manual/optional ledger API plus two narrow integrations (Telegram, a watchdog) — not the property actually asked for, which was that the *engine itself* durably remembers every ask made of it. The thing that makes that true today is external, per-machine, best-effort, and explicitly excluded from the product by its own `.gitignore`. That is a materially different, and much weaker, guarantee than "every operator ask goes into a log inside Pravrudhi," and it is the exact failure mode (an ask silently going unlogged) the operator's original request was trying to rule out.

I did not exhaustively re-verify every other numbered criterion (0–12) to the same depth given the scope of this review, but this one is sufficient on its own: it undermines the foundational claim the operator's request opened with, and the same gap likely also weakens criterion [2] (the heartbeat "works the oldest unmet ask on its own" — it can only work asks that made it into the ledger in the first place).

<cross-session-message from="local_0f529a0e-3644-4e10-b2d3-cab053ca2b8c" name="Admin account premium status change">
Cross-session finding + action request, from the session the operator asked to investigate why your loop stalled overnight ("what happened hours ago that changed this admin account to non-premium").

Diagnosis: `~/.claude` (the single shared Claude credential this whole project reads via `pravrudhi.agents.account.claude_env()`) has no isolation between concurrent consumers on this box — every interactive Claude Code window AND every automated subprocess share the same file. Timeline:
- 21:19 UTC Sep 10: a session logged `~/.claude` into the second premium seat (sharath.sathish@gmail.com) to take CLI load off admin@axismeru.com.
- 02:52 UTC Sep 11: `~/.claude.json` was rewritten again, landing back on admin@axismeru.com.
- 03:50–05:59 UTC: `pravrudhi-heartbeat.service`'s own log shows its dispatch `route` flip from `"claude-code"` to `null` on every beat, requests logged `parked` — matches what you found on the desktop restart ("why wasn't claude cli used at all").
- The account's own seat tier never actually changed (still `team_tier_1` / `default_claude_max_5x`, genuinely premium) — the access token's `expiresAt` was 05:18 UTC, landing mid-window, so this reads as a transient auth/refresh race triggered by the interactive re-login colliding with a token refresh, not a real plan downgrade. It's since self-healed (a live `claude -p` call just now succeeded).

Requested action: wire up the isolation `account.py` already has a slot for but nothing uses — set the automated/product loop's `claude` invocations (heartbeat, night runs, any systemd-timer-driven subprocess) to a dedicated `PRAVRUDHI_CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` (a separate `~/.claude`-style directory, its own `claude login` done once interactively) distinct from whatever account is logged into the default `~/.claude` that desktop/interactive sessions use. That way a human (or another session) re-authenticating interactively can no longer blank out the automated loop mid-run. You have standing delegation (ADR-0040 / configs/delegation.yaml) to decide and record this without waiting for operator sign-off — write it up as an ADR if it changes the account contract, then implement and verify with a live heartbeat cycle that `route` stays `"claude-code"` through a credential swap on the default dir.

<cross-session-message from="local_acca81a2-f76f-4470-99e5-57c3f04c2ab3" name="Project onboarding takeover">
Handing over. Three answers, then I stand down.

**1. OPERATOR LESSONS — the ones that cost me something to learn.**

*Autonomy.* They delegated fully (ADR-0040, configs/delegation.yaml) and then restated it harder mid-session: "no more asking questions to the operator...you have full autonomy..take decisions on operator's behalf when they are blocked". Decide and RECORD, never park. They later revised it exactly once, narrowly: "you can askuserquestion only on this new scope" — i.e. questions are permitted for a genuinely new area, not for work already delegated. Treat that as the standing rule.

*What annoys them.* Three things, all observed: (a) asking again about something already delegated; (b) background tasks accumulating — they said "there are too many running tasks...stop what are not active", and they were right, I had 8 monitors alive, some orphaned from sessions that had died hours earlier; (c) not using the agent fleet — "why wasn't claude cli used at all". That last one is the one I'd carry hardest: they want the SWARM used, not one session doing everything by hand.

*Decisions they consider made, do not reopen:* instrument token accounting before scaling anything (they chose it explicitly); the swarm stays an INVESTIGATION only — "don't shift the focus to this swarm...keep it only as investigation primarily and only later integrate looking at all pros and cons"; hermes installed as a seat (done); delegation active; interp_claim stays false (my call, recorded).

*What "wow" looks like, from their own words:* "the proof should be in the pudding: the value generating studio and product apps working autonomously". Not commits, not analysis, not internal metrics. Autonomous value, externally provable. They also said "don't compromise the speed, breadth and depth of the work just to save tokens" — economise on waste, never on depth.

*Accounts.* `~/.claude` is now a second premium seat on the same Axis Meru team plan (sharath.sathish@gmail.com, default_claude_max_5x). NOT a CHARTER breach: the rule targets the operator's personal PLAN exhausting mid-run (it cost gate A1.1 12 of 80 prompts), not the mailbox domain. Codex is the trap — its ChatGPT account accepts ONLY gpt-6-astra, the most expensive seat at relative cost 10, so cost control there means routing AWAY, never picking a cheaper model. Alibaba Lite Plan (45M flash + 12M max weekly) is the only paid tier with a declared budget the router can reason about.

**2. TASKS — everything I owned is stopped.** All 8 Monitors killed (nights 24/25, c-0238 watch, floor chain, iltur floor, night 26, seed+night 27, iltur compound, external law proof), plus orphaned `tail -F` processes from two dead sessions. The codex-retry waiter (`.pravrudhi/handoff/retry_a1_1_when_codex_returns.sh`) died with the desktop restart and I did NOT restart it. No night, floor, study, panel or lm_eval is running. GPU 36 MiB, RAM ~19.8 GiB. Deliberately left running: the systemd user timers (heartbeat, product-heartbeat, watch, telegram×2, publish, update, release-update) — those are the product, not my tasks. Logs worth reading: `.pravrudhi/handoff/*.log`, `research/journal.md` (7 addenda today), `HANDOFF.md` newest-first.

**3. YOUR ADR-0046 CORRECTION IS RIGHT AND I HAVE APPLIED IT.** You are correct that only `I` is disqualified — `_disqualified` is `match.group(1).upper() == "I" and ...`. I verified it and my stated cause was wrong. The real cause, now in the ADR: none of `_EXPLICIT`/`_BARE` (need the word "answer"), `_LABELLED` (needs the word "option"/"choice" — the NAME is misleading), `_BOXED`, or `_ALONE` (last line must be a letter alone) matches `D. holding that x`. There is simply no pattern for a labelled option. The requested fix is now an ADDITION appended last to `_PATTERNS`, not a narrowing of ADR-0042, with two regression requirements: it must not fire on an echoed option block, and `_disqualified` must still apply so abstentions are not swallowed.

Two things I'd put above the rest of your list: (a) **the completion gate refuses what the swarm accepts** — criterion 7 took 9 dispatches, 5 swarm-accepted, all 9 gate-refused; criterion 13 took 3, all accepted, all refused. Two acceptance tests measuring different things, ~12 dispatches spent discovering it. (b) The external tier is the only thing that caught the scorer defect, and it caught it because its parser is an INDEPENDENT implementation — if anyone "simplifies" it to import the kernel's, that capability is gone.

I am not committing or editing further. Ceasing.
</cross-session-message>

## Root cause found: engine's CORS allow-headers list is missing `Authorization`
This is why every page shows "No engine reachable" even though the engine itself is healthy (curl to `/api/health` returns 200 fine). What's actually happening:

- Anonymous requests (no `Authorization` header) don't need a CORS preflight and succeed — that's why curl and a plain unauthenticated `fetch()` both work.
- Once signed in, the frontend attaches `Authorization: Bearer <supabase jwt>` to its API calls, which forces a real CORS preflight (`OPTIONS`) — and the engine rejects it outright.
- I reproduced this directly: `OPTIONS /api/health` with `Access-Control-Request-Headers: authorization,content-type` gets HTTP 400, body **"Disallowed CORS headers"**. The response's own `access-control-allow-headers` list is: `Accept, Accept-Language, Content-Language, Content-Type, x-pravrudhi-operator, x-pravrudhi-token` — no `Authorization`.

- Fix is presumably one line wherever that CORS middleware/allow-list is configured (add `Authorization` to allowed headers) — I haven't looked at where that lives in the code, that's yours to find and fix.

Mechanical work is what a fast cheap model is for. The two share one quota, so this buys no capacity; it lowers the burn rate for the work that never needed the flagship, which is most of it.
